As a result, delegation is mixed, and calls are not made through the regular {@link SerializerFactory} interface. Instead, they are made directly to {@link BasicSerializerFactory}.

Finally, because the serializer provider, rather than the factory, handles all caching, and because this factory has no configurable state, the factory is stateless. Therefore, a global singleton instance can be used.

Return only the document text, without a preamble or a closing remark. --- A {@code Scheduler} is an object that specifies an API for scheduling units of work provided in the form of {@link Runnable}s to be executed without delay (effectively as soon as possible), after a specified time delay or periodically and represents an abstraction over an asynchronous boundary that ensures these units of work get executed by some underlying task-execution scheme (such as custom Threads, event loop, {@link java.util.concurrent.Executor Executor} or Actor system) with some uniform properties and guarantees regardless of the particular underlying scheme.

You can get various standard, RxJava-specific instances of this class via the static methods of the {@link io.reactivex.rxjava3.schedulers.Schedulers} utility class.

The so-called {@link Worker}s of a {@code Scheduler} can be created via the {@link #createWorker()} method which allow the scheduling of multiple {@link Runnable} tasks in an isolated manner. {@code Runnable} tasks scheduled on a {@code Worker} are guaranteed to be executed sequentially and in a non-overlapping fashion. Abstract class that defines the API used by {@link ObjectMapper} (and other chained {@link JsonSerializer}s) to serialize objects of arbitrary types into JSON, using the provided {@link JsonGenerator}. Use {@link com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ser.std.StdSerializer} instead of this class, because it implements many optional methods defined here.

NOTE: The various serialize methods are never called with null values. The caller must handle null values, usually by calling {@link SerializerProvider#findNullValueSerializer} to obtain a serializer. This also means that custom serializers cannot be used directly to change the output produced when serializing null values.

If a serializer is an aggregate one—meaning that it delegates handling of some content to other serializers—it typically also needs to implement {@link com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ser.ResolvableSerializer}, which can locate the required secondary serializers. This is important for allowing dynamic serializer overrides. A separate call interface is needed to separate resolution of secondary serializers, which may have a direct or indirect cyclic link back to the serializer itself.

To support per-property annotations, which configure serialization aspects on a per-property basis, serializers may also want to implement {@link com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ser.ContextualSerializer}. This interface allows serializer specialization: the call to {@link com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ser.ContextualSerializer#createContextual} receives property information and can create a newly configured serializer for handling that particular property.

If both {@link com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ser.ResolvableSerializer} and {@link com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ser.ContextualSerializer} are implemented, serializer resolution occurs before contextualization.

A {@code Scheduler} is an object that defines an API for scheduling units of work, provided as {@link Runnable}s, for execution without delay (effectively as soon as possible), after a specified delay, or periodically. It represents an abstraction over an asynchronous boundary that ensures these units of work are executed by an underlying task-execution scheme, such as custom threads, an event loop, a {@link java.util.concurrent.Executor Executor}, or an Actor system. The scheduler provides uniform properties and guarantees regardless of the underlying scheme.

You can obtain standard, RxJava-specific instances of this class through the static methods of the {@link io.reactivex.rxjava3.schedulers.Schedulers} utility class.

A {@code Scheduler}'s so-called {@link Worker}s can be created with the {@link #createWorker()} method. A {@code Worker} allows multiple {@link Runnable} tasks to be scheduled in isolation. {@code Runnable} tasks scheduled on a {@code Worker} are guaranteed to execute sequentially and without overlap. Non-delayed {@code Runnable} tasks are guaranteed to execute in First-In-First-Out order, although their execution may be interleaved with delayed tasks. Outstanding or running tasks can be cancelled together with {@link Worker#dispose()} without affecting any other {@code Worker} instances belonging to the same {@code Scheduler}.

Implementations of {@link #scheduleDirect} and {@link Worker#schedule} are encouraged to call {@link io.reactivex.rxjava3.plugins.RxJavaPlugins#onSchedule(Runnable)}. This allows a scheduler hook to manipulate, wrap, or replace the original {@code Runnable} task before it is submitted to the underlying task-execution scheme.

The default implementations of the {@code scheduleDirect} methods in this abstract class delegate each submitted {@code Runnable} task to the corresponding {@code schedule} method of a {@code Worker} created through {@link #createWorker()}. Implementations of this class are encouraged to provide a more efficient direct-scheduling implementation to avoid the time and memory overhead of creating a {@code Worker} for every task. This delegation uses special wrapper instances around the original {@code Runnable} before calling the corresponding {@code Worker.schedule} method. As a result, multiple {@code RxJavaPlugins.onSchedule} calls may occur, and multiple hooks may potentially be applied. Therefore, the default implementations of {@code scheduleDirect} and {@link Worker#schedulePeriodically(Runnable, long, long, TimeUnit)} wrap the incoming {@code Runnable} in a class that implements {@link io.reactivex.rxjava3.schedulers.SchedulerRunnableIntrospection}. This interface can provide access to the original or hooked {@code Runnable}. A repeated {@code RxJavaPlugins.onSchedule} call can then detect an earlier hook and avoid applying another hook to the same task.

The default implementations of {@link #now(TimeUnit)} and {@link Worker#now(TimeUnit)} return the current {@link System#currentTimeMillis()} value in the requested time unit. Custom {@code Scheduler} implementations can override these methods to provide specialized time accounting, such as virtual time that can be advanced programmatically. Operators requiring a {@code Scheduler} may rely on either the {@code now()} method provided by {@code Scheduler} or the one provided by {@code Worker}. Therefore, both methods should represent a logically consistent source of the current time.

The default implementation of {@link Worker#schedulePeriodically(Runnable, long, long, TimeUnit)} uses {@link Worker#schedule(Runnable, long, TimeUnit)} to schedule the {@code Runnable} task periodically. The default implementations of {@link #start()} and {@link #shutdown()} do nothing. They should be overridden when the underlying task-execution scheme supports stopping and restarting itself.

If a {@code Scheduler} is shut down or a {@code Worker} is disposed, the {@code schedule} methods should return the {@link Disposable#disposed()} singleton, indicating the shut-down or disposed state to the caller. Shutdown or disposal can occur from any thread. Consequently, if shutdown or disposal is detected after a task has been submitted to the underlying task-execution scheme, the scheduling implementations should make every effort to cancel that task immediately.

All methods on the {@code Scheduler} and {@code Worker} classes should be thread-safe.

Post-completion backpressure handles the case when a source produces values based on requests when it is active but more values are available even after its completion. In this case, the onComplete() can't just emit the contents of the queue but has to coordinate with the requested amounts. This requires two distinct modes: active and completed. In active mode, requests flow through and the queue is not accessed but in completed mode, requests no-longer reach the upstream but help in draining the queue.

The algorithm utilizes the most significant bit (bit 63) of a long value (AtomicLong) since request amount only goes up to {@link Long#MAX_VALUE} (bits 0-62) and negative values aren't allowed.

In this case, the onComplete() can't just emit the contents of the queue but has to coordinate with the requested amounts. This requires two distinct modes: active and completed. Abstract class that defines the API used by {@link ObjectMapper} (and other chained {@link JsonSerializer}s) to serialize objects of arbitrary types into JSON using the provided {@link JsonGenerator}. Use {@link com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ser.std.StdSerializer} instead of this class, since it implements many of this class's optional methods.

NOTE: The various serialize methods are never called with null values. The caller must handle null values, usually by calling {@link SerializerProvider#findNullValueSerializer} to obtain a serializer to use. This also means that custom serializers cannot be used directly to change the output produced when serializing null values.

If a serializer is an aggregate one—meaning that it delegates the handling of some of its contents to other serializers—it typically also needs to implement {@link com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ser.ResolvableSerializer}, which can locate the required secondary serializers. This is important for allowing dynamic serializer overrides; a separate call interface is needed to separate the resolution of secondary serializers, which may have a cyclic link back to the serializer itself, directly or indirectly.

In addition, to support per-property annotations that configure serialization aspects on a per-property basis, serializers may want to implement {@link com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ser.ContextualSerializer}. This allows serializer specialization: the call to {@link com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ser.ContextualSerializer#createContextual} receives information about the property and can create a newly configured serializer for handling that particular property.

If both {@link com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ser.ResolvableSerializer} and {@link com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ser.ContextualSerializer} are implemented, serializer resolution occurs before contextualization.

All methods are safe to call from multiple threads, but note that there is no guarantee whose terminal event will win and get delivered to the downstream.

Calling {@link #onComplete()} multiple times has no effect. Calling {@link #onError(Throwable)} multiple times or after {@code onComplete} will route the exception into the global error handler via {@link io.reactivex.rxjava3.plugins.RxJavaPlugins#onError(Throwable)}.

The emitter allows the registration of a single resource, in the form of a {@link Disposable} or {@link Cancellable} via {@link #setDisposable(Disposable)} or {@link #setCancellable(Cancellable)} respectively. The emitter implementations will dispose/cancel this instance when the downstream cancels the flow or after the event generator logic calls {@link #onError(Throwable)}, {@link #onComplete()} or when {@link #tryOnError(Throwable)} succeeds.

Only one {@code Disposable} or {@code Cancellable} object can be associated with the emitter at a time. Calling either {@code set} method will dispose/cancel any previous object. If there is a need for handling multiple resources, one can create a {@link io.reactivex.rxjava3.disposables.CompositeDisposable} and associate that with the emitter instead.

The {@link Cancellable} is logically equivalent to {@code Disposable} but allows using cleanup logic that can throw a checked exception (such as many {@code close()} methods on Java IO components). Since the release of resources happens after the terminal events have been delivered or the sequence gets cancelled, exceptions throw within {@code Cancellable} are routed to the global error handler via {@link io.reactivex.rxjava3.plugins.RxJavaPlugins#onError(Throwable)}.
